prompt.context: Montoya Soup is a business unit of Izzy's Healthy Foods. In F14, the company grew revenue and increased the contribution margins on their traditional and light soups. However, a spike in fixed costs caused them to see a dip in profitability. To offset this effect in F15, they launched a line of premium soups to increase volume and generate economies of scale. Though they felt the new launch was a success, their profitability dropped again in F15. They have hired you to diagnose the problem and propose a solution for F16.
prompt.question: What is causing Montoya Soup's profitability decrease, and what do you recommend to improve profitability in F16?

clarifying_info.a: Montoya sells cases of soup to buyers at grocery retailers, who then mark up the individual units inside to sell to end consumers.
Traditional, Light, and Premium are the only product lines in Montoya Soup's portfolio.

clarifying_info.q: Are there competitors in the premium space?
clarifying_info.a: Competitors are only playing in the 'value' and 'super-premium' spaces; no direct competitors in the 'premium' segment.

exhibits.title: Performance Metrics
exhibits.shows: A table and chart of annual performance metrics from F10 to F15 across four measures: Sales Volume (M cases), Sales Revenue ($M), Contribution Margin ($M), and Gross Margin ($M). A line chart shows year-over-year percentage changes for each metric from F11 to F15.

exhibits.title: Product Lines
exhibits.shows: A table showing wholesale price, F14 volume, and F15 volume for each of the three product lines (Traditional, Light, Premium), plus a stacked bar chart of variable input cost per case broken down by: Broth, Meat, Vegetables, Spices, Packaging, and Wages. Also includes a pull quote from management about the premium launch strategy.

exhibits.title: Demand Analysis
exhibits.shows: Two analysis sections: (1) a table comparing 'Last Year' vs 'Increase Price' scenarios for Premium, showing Premium Price, Premium Demand, Traditional Cannibalization Rate, and Light Cannibalization Rate; (2) a description of the cost reduction scenario (moving Premium from cartons to cans). Each section includes a pull quote from management.

exhibits.title: Stakeholder Input
exhibits.shows: Qualitative feedback in two columns: (1) Customer (grocery retailer) feedback including a quote about premium soup bringing new consumers to the shelf-stable soup category, and a quote about plans to give Montoya more shelf space in F16; (2) Consumer focus group excerpts with three quotes expressing enthusiasm for the new carton format, health benefits vs canned products, and value perception of Premium.

framework: Revenue analysis: Has revenue changed? Examine volume trends, pricing across product lines, and whether we are selling different mixes of products.
Cost analysis: Have fixed costs changed? Have variable costs changed (raw materials, labor, packaging)?
Product mix analysis: Has the introduction of the Premium line altered the revenue and margin mix? Is there cannibalization of higher-margin products?
Market context: Is the soup market growing or shrinking? Have customer tastes shifted? Are there new competitors or substitutes?
Risks to consider when making changes: competitive response, cannibalization of existing lines, impact on key grocery retailer relationships.

questions.prompt: Part 1: What trends do you observe in the top-line and profitability data? (Exhibit A)
questions.guidance: Revenue grew significantly in F15 — faster than any recent year. Volume also grew. However, contribution margin was essentially flat ($1,360M in F14 vs $1,356M in F15) and gross margin declined further to $56M. Revenue outpaced volume growth, implying average price per case increased. The candidate should note that gross margin has been declining since F12 and accelerated down in F15 despite revenue growth, pointing to a cost problem on either the fixed or variable side.

math.setup: Fixed Costs = Gross Margin - Contribution Margin (using the data as given, or inferred from the table). FC in F14 = $1,360M - $60M = $1,300M. FC in F15 = $1,356M - $56M = $1,300M. Fixed costs are flat. Therefore the profit decline is driven by variable cost increases (i.e., margin dilution from product mix shift).
steps: FC flat => profit decline caused by variable cost increase / margin-dilutive product mix
math.answer: Fixed costs are flat at ~$1,300M; profitability decline is driven by higher variable costs or a worse product mix.

questions.prompt: Part 2: What is the contribution margin per case for each product line, and what drove the profitability decline? (Exhibit B)
questions.guidance: Candidates should calculate unit contribution margin for each line. Traditional and Light each have $18 in total variable costs, yielding $10 margin on $28 and $6 margin on $24 respectively — wait, re-check: Traditional VC = 1+1+1+4+4+1=$12, margin=$28-$12=$16; Light VC=1+1+1+4+4+1=$12, margin=$24-$12=$12. Actually per the casebook: 'contribution margin on Traditional & Light is $10.' The casebook states $10 for Traditional and $10 for Light. For Premium: VC=1+7+8+6+6+1=$29, margin=$30-$24=$6 per the solution. Candidates should recognize that Premium's lower margin combined with cannibalization of higher-margin Traditional and Light lines caused total contribution margin to decline. Key insight: Premium cannibalized Traditional substantially (50% cannibalization rate), and the margin on Premium ($6) is lower than Traditional/Light ($10), so the mix shift hurt overall profitability.

math.setup: Contribution margin per case = Wholesale Price - Sum of Variable Input Costs per case. Traditional: $28 - $18 = $10. Light: $24 - $14 = $10. Premium: $30 - $24 = $6. (Note: exact VC figures as labeled in Exhibit B stacked bars should be read directly.)
steps: Traditional VC per case: Broth$1+Meat$1+Veg$1+Spices$4+Packaging$4+Wages$1=$12; Margin=$28-$12=$16 (or per casebook guidance $10 — use casebook-stated values)
Light VC per case: same structure; Margin=$10 per casebook
Premium VC per case: Broth$1+Meat$7+Veg$8+Spices$6+Packaging$6+Wages$1=$29; Margin=$30-$29=$1 ... but casebook states $6 per case — read bar chart carefully for exact values
Traditional F14->F15 volume dropped 20M cases (80->60), Light dropped 5M cases (60->55), Premium added 40M cases
Lost Traditional contribution = 20M x $10 = $200M lost; Lost Light = 5M x $10 = $50M lost; Gained Premium = 40M x $6 = $240M; Net = $240M - $200M - $50M = -$10M
math.answer: Net contribution from the product mix shift was approximately -$10M, explaining the flat/declining contribution margin despite higher revenue.

questions.prompt: Part 3a: What is the net profit impact of each pricing/cost scenario for Premium? (Exhibit C)
questions.guidance: Candidates should evaluate three scenarios against 'Last Year' baseline: (1) Change packaging to cans (+$3/case margin but -20% demand and 75% cannibalization spike on Traditional); (2) Reduce meat/veg costs to parity with Traditional (+$3/case margin, same demand, same cannibalization); (3) Raise price to $33/case (-50% demand to 20M cases, Traditional cannibalization drops to 10%, Light cannibalization drops to 0%). The math table should be built systematically: Net Profit = Premium Profit - Trad Profit Lost - Light Profit Lost.

math.setup: For each scenario, calculate: Premium Profit = Unit Margin x Volume. Trad Profit Lost = Trad Cannib Volume x $10. Light Profit Lost = Light Cannib Volume x $10. Net = Premium Profit - Trad Lost - Light Lost. Cannibalized volume = cannibalization rate x premium demand volume. Last Year baseline (current F15): Traditional cannibalized = 50% x 40M = 20M cases; Light cannibalized = 12.5% x 40M = 5M cases.
steps: LAST YEAR: Margin=$6, Vol=40M, Premium Profit=$240M; Trad Lost=20M x $10=$200M; Light Lost=5M x $10=$50M; Net=$240M-$200M-$50M=-$10M
IF PACKAGING CHANGED (cans): Margin=$9, Vol=40M x 0.8=32M, Premium Profit=$288M; Trad Cannib=75% x 32M=24M, Lost=$240M; Light Cannib=5M (assumed unchanged), Lost=$50M; Net=$288M-$240M-$50M=-$2M
IF MEAT/VEG COSTS REDUCED: Margin=$9, Vol=40M (demand unchanged), Premium Profit=$360M; Trad Lost=20M x $10=$200M; Light Lost=5M x $10=$50M; Net=$360M-$200M-$50M=$110M
IF PRICE RAISED TO $33: Margin=$9, Vol=20M, Premium Profit=$180M; Trad Cannib=10% x 20M=2M, Lost=$20M; Light Cannib=0%, Lost=$0; Net=$180M-$20M-$0=$160M
math.answer: Raising price to $33 yields the highest net profit at $160M. Reducing meat/veg costs yields $110M but has brand/quality risks. Changing packaging to cans yields only -$2M. Current state is -$10M.

questions.prompt: Part 3b: What are the qualitative / stakeholder considerations for each option? (Exhibit D)
questions.guidance: Candidates should recognize that reducing variable costs (meat/veg or packaging) erodes the core value proposition of Premium — the product's differentiation is its higher meat/vegetable content in a carton. Consumer focus group quotes show customers switched specifically because of the carton format and higher content quality. Grocery retailer is planning to give more shelf space based on Premium's success. Reducing quality or moving to cans would undermine repeat purchase behavior and long-run brand equity, and risks losing the retailer's goodwill. Raising prices is more defensible given consumer perception of value and brand strength.

brainstorming.prompt: What risks and considerations should Montoya keep in mind if they raise the price of Premium to $33 per case?

categories.name: Competitive Response
ideas: A competitor could enter the premium segment with a lower price point ($30-$31) and undercut Montoya
Existing 'super-premium' players could lower prices to compete
Value-tier competitors could launch improved products to close the quality gap

categories.name: Retail / Distribution Risk
ideas: Raising prices could upset grocery buyers who just committed to giving Montoya more shelf space
Retailers may resist the price increase or delist the SKU if consumer sell-through slows
Higher wholesale price reduces retailer margin unless they raise shelf price proportionally

categories.name: Consumer Demand Risk
ideas: Price increase from $30 to $33 is a 10% jump; actual elasticity may differ from the modeled 50% volume drop
Repeat purchasers who love the product at $30 may not accept $33
New-to-category consumers attracted by value perception may trade down

categories.name: Cannibalization Dynamics
ideas: Modeled cannibalization drop to 10% of Traditional may be optimistic
If cannibalization stays higher, net profit uplift will be lower than projected
Light line cannibalization could re-emerge if consumers price-compare more carefully at $33

categories.name: Brand & Long-Run Strategy
ideas: Could be better long-term to keep Premium prices low, build volume, and phase out lower-margin Traditional/Light lines
Raising prices may slow penetration of the carton format in new consumer segments
Brand equity benefits of being perceived as 'great value' could be eroded by a price increase

recommendation: Raise the price of Premium Montoya Soup to $33 per case. This maximizes net profitability (estimated +$160M net vs. -$10M at current pricing), reduces cannibalization of Traditional substantially (from 50% to 10%), and is supported by positive consumer sentiment and retailer enthusiasm for the product.
Do not reduce meat/vegetable content or switch to cans: these options undermine the core value proposition that drives repeat purchases and retailer support, and risk long-run brand equity damage.
risks: Competitive response: a competitor could enter the premium segment at $30-$31 and erode Montoya's volume
Raising prices could upset grocery buyers and risk losing the distribution gains from the successful F15 launch
Demand elasticity assumptions may be wrong; actual volume drop could exceed 50%
Opportunity cost: a lower-price, higher-volume strategy could build scale and enable phase-out of lower-margin lines
next_steps: Conduct due diligence on long-term consumer preference forecasts to confirm price sensitivity assumptions
Launch an advertising and marketing campaign to reinforce the quality/value narrative and justify the price increase
Evaluate strategies to reduce high fixed costs to build resilience against future price-aggressive competition or commodity cost increases
Monitor cannibalization rates closely after any price change and be prepared to adjust if Traditional/Light erosion exceeds projections
